parts.part: castle (eastern, higher subdivision of the citadel)
parts.layout_phase: Stage I (first fortification); made into the 'castle' and given its monumental gates in Stage III (IIIA)
parts.what_was_built: The castle stands on the first settlement at the site. Bisht's final account says 'The remains of the first settlement belonging to Stage I lie buried beneath the castle. It was enclosed by a massive fortification wall', whose southern arm, cut near the south-western corner, had a basal width of 11 m and an extant height of about 6.5 m, and he adds that 'The foundation of planning that was laid in Stage I formed the nucleus on which the subsequent settlements of the later stages expanded into a full-fledged city' (Bisht 2015, p. 95). The 1991-92 season report calls the Stage I settlement 'a formidable fortress probably with four walls' with a southern wall of 11.10 m basal width built of rubble in mud mortar with sparing use of 36 x 18 x 9 cm mud-bricks (IAR 1991-92, p. 26). In Stage II a 2.80 m mud-brick wall was added to the inner face of this wall; in Stage III a further 4.5 m of brick masonry was added and 'the pre-existing walled settlement was made into a castle' while the bailey was added on the west (Bisht 2015, pp. 97, 99). 'The monumental gateways of the Castle and the appertenent terraces had come into existence in Stage III' (IAR 1991-92, p. 28). The line of the castle walls therefore dates from Stage I, while the walls, gates and terraces exposed today are the Stage III enlargement of it, repaired after the earthquake that closed Stage IIIA.
parts.excavator_basis: Bisht's chronology table gives Stage I as c. 3000-2900 BCE (Bisht 2015, pp. 104-105). He says the table was built 'Keeping in view of stratigraphical sequence, position and basic cultural forms' (p. 104), and on p. 99 compares the pottery of Stages I and II with Amri IIB, 'datable to the early part of third millennium BCE'. The range is therefore a stratigraphic and ceramic cross-dating estimate. No radiocarbon or thermoluminescence date is attached to Stage I; of the four thermoluminescence dates from the Physical Research Laboratory, the two that Bisht prints are for Stages II and III (see the bailey part).

syntheses.statement: From radiocarbon dates on archaeological carbonates from all seven stages the authors place 'the beginning of occupation at ~5500 years BP (pre-Harappan), and continuation until ~3800 years BP (early part of the Late Harappan period)'. Only the abstract could be read; the dated samples, their stage attributions and the calibration are in the paper and its supplementary Table S4, which we could not obtain.
syntheses.disagreement: If ~5500 years BP is read as calendar years before AD 1950, the start of occupation falls near 3550 BCE, about five centuries before Bisht's c. 3000 BCE for Stage I. The abstract does not say whether the ages are calibrated, so the size of the difference is uncertain.

syntheses.statement: Rawat, a member of Bisht's excavation team, writes: 'According to the excavator, the seven cultural stages of Dholavira can be dated between 3500 and 1700 bc.'
syntheses.disagreement: This attributes to the excavator a start about five centuries earlier and an end about 250 years earlier than the table in Bisht 2015 (Stage I c. 3000-2900 BCE, Stage VII c. 1500-1450 BCE). Rawat gives no basis or reference for the figures.

syntheses.statement: Bisht and co-authors reprint the stage table 'after Bisht 2015: 104', with Stage I c. 3000-2900 BCE and Stages I to III all labelled 'Early Harappan (Dholavira culture)'; Stage IV (c. 2500-2100 BCE) is the first stage labelled 'Mature Harappan'.

parts.conflicts: The excavator's account of the first fortification changed over the first three seasons. After the 1989-90 season the first occupation (layers 10 to 7, 65 to 70 cm thick) was described as 'a non-Harappan or pre-Harappan culture' lying under 'the hitherto known first defensive wall which is named as IA'; no wall of that phase had been found, and an earlier enclosure wall concealed under Wall IA was only inferred (IAR 1989-90, p. 16; Bisht 1991, p. 76, where he also wrote that it 'remains still uncertain' whether Harappans built the first fortification). The 1990-91 season exposed that earlier wall, 11.20 m wide at the base and faced with stone, and reassigned Wall IA to the second phase (IAR 1990-91, pp. 10-11). From 1991-92 the first phase is Stage I and its fortress is the start of the castle (IAR 1991-92, p. 26). In 1999 Bisht withdrew the 'Non-Harappan' or 'Pre-Harappan' label for Stage I and called it a formative stage of the Harappan culture (Bisht 1999, p. 22). The absolute dates also disagree: Bisht 2015 gives c. 3000-2900 BCE, Rawat reports the excavator's span as beginning in 3500 BC, and Sengupta and colleagues' carbonate dates put first occupation near 5500 years BP.

parts.what_was_built: In Stage IIIA 'The existing fortress was enlarged into two divisions, namely Castle and Bailey, the former on the relics of the earlier fortress while the latter added to it from the west, both being fortified' (IAR 1991-92, p. 28). The final report repeats that in Stage III 'another walled subdivision, arbitrarily called as bailey, was added to it from the west' (Bisht 2015, p. 99), and its conclusions state that 'the Bailey and Middle Town and Multi-purpose grounds along with their fortification systems came into being in Stage III' (p. 890). The bailey's fortification was built against the western arm of the castle wall (p. 891); its interior measures 120 by 120 m (p. 107). The earthquake at the end of Stage IIIA was followed by repairs and modifications of the layout 'particularly at Castle, Bailey, and Middle Town' (p. 890).
parts.locator: iar1991-92 p. 28; bisht2015dholavira pp. 99, 107, 890-891; bisht1999puratattva p. 22
parts.excavator_basis: Bisht gives Stage III as c. 2800-2500 BCE and does not divide the range between IIIA and IIIB (Bisht 2015, p. 104). The table rests on stratigraphy and ceramic cross-dating (p. 104). Beside Stage III he prints a thermoluminescence date from the Physical Research Laboratory, 'DHR 93/TL/4 2809±461 BCE', and beside Stage II 'DHR 93/TL/8 2302±480 BCE'; of four thermoluminescence dates two were 'erratic', the Stage III date 'falls consistently', and the Stage II date is 'not consistent with the chronology developed based on stratigraphical and typological considerations' (pp. 104-105). These are thermoluminescence dates on unspecified samples, not radiocarbon determinations.

syntheses.statement: 'The settlement rapidly expanded under favourable monsoonal climate conditions when architectural elements such as the Citadel, Bailey, Lower and Middle Town were added between the Early and mid-Mature Harappan periods.' The abstract gives no dates for these additions.
syntheses.disagreement: No numerical conflict can be checked from the abstract. Bisht places the bailey, middle town and ceremonial ground in Stage IIIA and the lower town in Stage IIIB, and Bisht and co-authors label Stage III 'Early Harappan (Dholavira culture)'; the abstract's 'between the Early and mid-Mature Harappan periods' allows some of these additions to be later than Stage III.

syntheses.statement: Stage III c. 2800-2500 BCE, labelled 'Early Harappan (Dholavira culture)'.

parts.conflicts: None on the stage of construction: the 1991-92 season report, Bisht 1999 and Bisht 2015 all put the bailey in Stage III, and the season report specifies IIIA.

parts.part: ceremonial ground (the 'stadium', multipurpose ground or great ground between the citadel and the middle town)
parts.what_was_built: In Stage IIIA 'The northern extension of the preceding stage was cleared of its structures and transformed into a Stadium which was bounded by stepped terraces meant for the spectators' (IAR 1991-92, p. 28). Bisht's conclusions add that 'This plaza came into existence certainly in Stage IIIA and maintained as such, all throughout the occupation of the site, although underneath these floors, there are found some structures along with the pottery of Stage II' (Bisht 2015, p. 892). The great ground measures 283 to 285 m by 45 to 47.50 m and is enclosed by the fortifications of the citadel and the middle town, with gates and tiers of seating along its sides (pp. 107, 124-125).
parts.excavator_basis: Stage III range of Bisht 2015, p. 104 (stratigraphy and ceramic cross-dating, with the single Stage III thermoluminescence date DHR 93/TL/4 2809±461 BCE); no sub-range is given for IIIA.
parts.conflicts: The ground overlies Stage II houses: the residential area that grew north of the walled settlement in Stage II was cleared to make it (Bisht 2015, pp. 97, 99, 892). The occupation of this area therefore begins in Stage II, while the open layout begins in Stage IIIA.

parts.what_was_built: 'The Middle Town was founded to the north of the Stadium with a separate fortification, furnished with bastions, corner towers and gateways' in Stage IIIA (IAR 1991-92, p. 28). The final report says that in Stage III 'the extensive walled town (which would become middle town subsequently) was founded' (Bisht 2015, p. 99), and the schematic section of the divisions shows the middle-town deposit beginning with Stage IIIA (Fig. 5.2, p. 97). In trench 45 x 43, dug to natural soil at 8.55 m, 'the habitation started here in early stage of stage III' (p. 129). Its fortified interior measures 340.5 by 242 m without the ground, laid out on an arterial street with staggered cross streets (pp. 107, 125-128). In Stage IIIA a built-up strip ran along its southern margin; it was cleared of structures in the following stage (p. 893).
parts.excavator_basis: Stage III range of Bisht 2015, p. 104 (stratigraphy and ceramic cross-dating, with the single Stage III thermoluminescence date DHR 93/TL/4 2809±461 BCE); no sub-range is given for IIIA.

syntheses.statement: The middle town is among the elements 'added between the Early and mid-Mature Harappan periods'.
syntheses.disagreement: See the bailey part: the abstract's bracket is broader than Bisht's Stage IIIA and gives no dates.

parts.conflicts: Bisht 1991 (p. 72), written after the first season, describes the middle town as one of three principal divisions without dating its foundation; the stage attribution comes from the 1991-92 season onward and is consistent thereafter.

parts.part: outer fortification (city wall enclosing all divisions)
parts.layout_phase: Stage IIIA; extended eastward in Stage IIIB
parts.what_was_built: In Stage IIIA 'The entire settlement consisted of the bipartite citadel, stadium, new-built residential division and the surrounding reservoirs, secured firmly by a circumvallation which, in turn, was reinforced with bastions and towers' with broad roads running round the walls; after the earthquake that began Stage IIIB 'the city walls were also extended further eastward in order to encompass the new division' (IAR 1991-92, p. 28). The final report: in Stage III 'finally, an outer fortification was raised to surround all the above components', and after the catastrophe 'the city-walls were extended further eastwards in order to enclose the new additions' (Bisht 2015, p. 99); 'The outer wall which was constructed in Stage III and remained in use throughout Stage IV and V and partly during Stage VI runs for a length of 781 m ... on the north and 630.50 m ... on the west' (p. 112; direction words omitted). The walls are of moulded mud-brick laid in receding courses, faced outside with rubble and hammer-dressed stone (p. 112); three corners with bastions were exposed in 1990-91 (IAR 1990-91, p. 12).
parts.locator: iar1991-92 p. 28; bisht2015dholavira pp. 99, 112-113, 130; bisht1999puratattva p. 24; iar1990-91 p. 12
parts.excavator_basis: Stage III range of Bisht 2015, p. 104 (stratigraphy and ceramic cross-dating, with the single Stage III thermoluminescence date DHR 93/TL/4 2809±461 BCE); no sub-range is given for IIIA or IIIB.
parts.conflicts: The eastern part of the circuit as it stands is a Stage IIIB extension of a Stage IIIA wall, so the wall is not of one build. The OCR text of Bisht 1999 reads 'Stage II' for the construction of the outer wall; the printed page (p. 24) reads 'Stage III', which we checked on the page image.

parts.what_was_built: 'The Stage III B followed a catastrophic earthquake that caused extensive devastation at the site. Large-scale repair works were undertaken. The Lower Town was added to the east of that division of the town that was founded in the Stage III A' (IAR 1991-92, p. 28). Bisht 2015 repeats that after the catastrophe 'the lower town was added' (p. 99), that 'the lower town came into existence during stage IIIB and survived through stage V' (p. 130), and that after the earthquake at the end of Stage IIIA 'the settlement, which was a town till then, assumed a full-fledged cityscape, when the Lower Town came into existence' (p. 890); the schematic section starts the lower-town deposit with Stage IIIB (Fig. 5.2, p. 97). The lower town has no wall of its own and lies within the outer fortification; its built-up area is 300 by 300 m, crossed by the continuation of the middle town's arterial street (pp. 107, 111, 130).
parts.locator: iar1991-92 p. 28; bisht2015dholavira pp. 97 (Fig. 5.2), 99, 111, 130, 890; bisht1999puratattva pp. 22, 25
parts.excavator_basis: Stage III range of Bisht 2015, p. 104; Stage IIIB is the last third of Stage III ('When the town of Stage III had lived two-thirds of its life, it was immensely damaged by a catastrophe', p. 99), but no separate range is printed for it.

syntheses.statement: The lower town is among the elements 'added between the Early and mid-Mature Harappan periods'.
syntheses.disagreement: See the bailey part: the abstract's bracket is broader than Bisht's Stage IIIB and gives no dates.

parts.conflicts: Bisht 1999 (p. 25) writes that the city-to-castle proportions 'were obtained by making alterations in the planning at the time when the lower town was added towards the close of stage III', which agrees with Stage IIIB. Bisht also reports that in Stage IIIB the earlier divisions were re-planned to new ratios (Bisht 1999, p. 22), so parts of the castle, bailey and middle town as exposed today may carry IIIB alterations.

parts.part: annexe (built-up area south of the castle along the southern city wall)
parts.what_was_built: The annexe is 'another built-up area, which rues along the city wall' south of the castle and its reservoirs, 'meant for housing perhaps warehouse and other specific uses' (Bisht 2015, p. 92). The 1991-92 season report lists it among the components of the cityscape attained 'By Stage III' (IAR 1991-92, p. 28). A wall running between the bailey and the annexe tied the castle into the outer fortification (Bisht 2015, p. 891).
parts.excavator_basis: Stage III range of Bisht 2015, p. 104 (stratigraphy and ceramic cross-dating).
parts.conflicts: Bisht 2015 is internally inconsistent about the annexe. On p. 92 it belongs to the fully developed city that Stages IV and V 'maintained as such', but the conclusions say that after the earthquake at the end of Stage IIIA 'at this point of time, Annexe was abandoned' (p. 890). If the second statement holds, the annexe was built no later than Stage IIIA and was not part of the Stage IIIB to V city.

first_occupation.basis: Bisht 2015 dates Stage I to c. 3000-2900 BCE from stratigraphy and ceramic cross-dating (pp. 99, 104-105). The Stage I deposit in the castle is 60 to 70 cm thick (Bisht 2015, p. 97, '65 – 60 cm'; IAR 1991-92, p. 28, '65-70 cm') and overlies sterile strata (IAR 1989-90, p. 16). Other statements of the start are later: Rawat 2015 (p. 199) reports the excavator's span as beginning in 3500 BC, and Sengupta and colleagues put the beginning of occupation at ~5500 years BP from carbonate radiocarbon dates (abstract).

notes: Dholavira was occupied before its town plan existed. Bisht divides the 11.30 m of occupation in the castle into seven stages (Bisht 2015, pp. 95-105). Stage I was already a walled settlement, and the castle's fortification line goes back to it. The planned city with its several walled divisions belongs to Stage III. In Stage IIIA the bailey, the ceremonial ground, the walled middle town and an outer wall round all of them were built. In Stage IIIB, after an earthquake, the lower town was added and the outer wall was extended east to enclose it (IAR 1991-92, p. 28; Bisht 2015, pp. 99, 890). We therefore record the castle with Stage I as its layout phase and the other divisions with Stage IIIA or IIIB. The only absolute ranges the excavator publishes are the stage ranges in his chronology table: Stage I c. 3000-2900 BCE, Stage II c. 2900-2800, Stage III c. 2800-2500, Stage IV c. 2500-2100 BCE (Bisht 2015, p. 104). He says they rest on stratigraphy and ceramic comparison, supported by one thermoluminescence date for Stage III (2809±461 BCE). We found no published radiocarbon determination with a laboratory number from any Dholavira stage. Bisht thanks D. P. Agrawal of the Physical Research Laboratory 'for helping in radiocarbon dates of five samples' (Bisht 2015, p. 3), but the report does not print them, and the Radiocarbon date lists PRL-I to PRL-VI and PRLC-I contain no Dholavira entry. Sengupta and colleagues (2020) dated archaeological carbonates from all seven stages, but their table is in a supplement behind the publisher's paywall; we record only their abstract. Two conference items by the same group were saved (data/raw/2026-10-21-town-axes/dating/dholavira/goldschmidt2020sengupta.pdf, egu22_254.pdf). The 2022 presentation quotes single AMS ages of 4647 and 5248 years BP for an 'Early Harappan' otolith and freshwater bivalve, without laboratory numbers, errors or stage, so we do not enter them as determinations. No Bayesian model of Dholavira's phase boundaries has been published as far as we could find. Possehl's compilations (1999, 2002) could not be consulted: the Internet Archive copy of The Indus Civilization (2002) is lending-only, and we did not find Indus Age: The Beginnings online. The Indian Archaeology reviews for the seasons after 1991-92 were not consulted. Bisht 2015 and Bisht 1999 state the orientation of the city; per our brief we ignored it.
